title: Choose Hyperion's palette world
question: Which material language should turn warm ivory and restrained gold into a working service hub?

options.label: The Service Atlas
options.lineage: surveyor field atlases, engraved wayfinding, and brass map pins
options.thesis: Hyperion becomes a calm map of the deployed world, with gold reserved for bearings and chosen routes.
options.viewport: A compact service index reads like an owned atlas: direct links lead, health marks the margin, and logs sit one layer deeper.
options.risk: Too much cartographic ornament would slow the quick-access job, so the map language must live in rules, labels, and states.

options.label: The Living Index
options.lineage: variable-type specimens and type foundry proof sheets
options.thesis: Every service is recognized by a bold typographic signature inside an unusually quiet working index.
options.case: Strong personal recognition and excellent scanability; less naturally expresses relationships between services than the atlas.
options.viewport: Large service initials anchor a disciplined list while tiny technical labels carry state, endpoint, and log access.
options.risk: The oversized lettering could feel editorial rather than operational if names vary wildly in length.

options.label: The Signal Grid
options.lineage: man-machine diagrams and strict traffic-control schematics
options.thesis: Services become nodes on a precise routing grid whose connections illuminate only when needed.
options.case: Best expression of a future communication hub, but its signal-red identity fights the requested ivory-and-gold restraint.
options.viewport: A compact orthogonal network keeps every service link in a fixed place and lights the selected route through the system.
options.risk: It can become visually busy and make the product look like a topology tool rather than a fast personal launcher.

options.label: The Status Instrument
options.lineage: seven-segment instruments and designed unlit display cells
options.thesis: Availability is rendered as an unmistakable instrument reading, with inactive states designed as carefully as active ones.
options.case: Instant status recognition is excellent; the dark instrument character and numeric bias fit the product less well.
options.viewport: Each service occupies a fixed instrument slot where state changes in place and the direct-access label remains stable.
options.risk: It overemphasizes monitoring even though opening services—not watching metrics—is Hyperion's primary job.

canonCard.label: The polished dashboard standard
canonCard.thesis: A familiar neutral admin dashboard with conventional cards and a muted gold brand accent.
canonCard.viewport: A sidebar and card grid expose service name, status, direct link, and log action in the expected arrangement.
canonCard.risk: Efficient and familiar, but it leaves Hyperion with little identity beyond its accent color.
